issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s omission to restore an essential supply that an authority disconnected can constitute withholding when the landlord could have restored it.
material_facts: The municipal water supply had been disconnected because the former owner had defaulted on municipal payments.
The current landlord was not responsible for the original default but could have had the connection restored by paying the prescribed fee.
The landlord did not arrange restoration of the water supply.
issues.conclusion: The landlord’s omission to restore the supply was attributable to him and constituted withholding an essential supply.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 24(1) and Explanation II of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, withholding includes an act or omission attributable to a landlord that causes an authority to cut off an essential supply. Water is an essential supply under Explanation I. An omission to take steps within the landlord’s power to restore the supply may therefore amount to withholding, even if the landlord did not cause the original disconnection.

rule.if: criminal_withholding_prosecution and authority_disconnected_essential_supply and landlord_could_restore_supply_by_payment and landlord_failed_to_restore_supply

predicates.criminal_withholding_prosecution: The proceeding seeks to punish a landlord for withholding an essential service from a tenant.
predicates.authority_disconnected_essential_supply: An authority disconnected an essential supply serving the rented premises.
predicates.landlord_could_restore_supply_by_payment: The landlord could have had the supply restored by making a required payment.
predicates.landlord_failed_to_restore_supply: The landlord did not take the available steps to restore the supply.

issues.definition: When an authority has disconnected an essential supply, a landlord’s failure to restore it despite being able to do so by payment counts as withholding in a criminal withholding prosecution.

issues.legal_issue: A criminal conviction for withholding an essential supply requires that the supply have been available for the tenant’s use at some time while the protective law was in force.
material_facts: The municipal water supply had been disconnected before the relevant law came into force.
The tenant remained in occupation but did not have the use of municipal water after the law came into force.
The tenant obtained water from a well instead, and the municipal connection was never restored during that period.
issues.conclusion: Because the tenant had not enjoyed the municipal water supply at any time while the law was in force, the offence was not established and the conviction and sentence were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 24(1), read with subsections (2) and (3), requires that the essential supply have been available for the tenant’s use at some time while the Act was in force. “Enjoyed” does not mean merely having a legal right to the supply, nor does enjoyment in the remote past before the Act suffice. Reading the provision otherwise would make previously non-penal conduct penal retrospectively, contrary to Article 20(1) of the Constitution. The Court also applied strict construction to the provision’s exceptional penal remedies.

predicates.criminal_withholding_prosecution: The proceeding seeks to punish a landlord for withholding an essential service from a tenant.
predicates.essential_supply_was_never_available_to_: The essential supply was not available for the tenant’s use at any time while the relevant protective law was in force.

issues.definition: In a criminal withholding prosecution, if the essential supply was never available for the tenant’s use while the law was in force, a conviction for withholding cannot stand.
